evaluation.positioning_hook: A border patrol officer and a Mexican drug lord are forced into an uneasy alliance when a sleeper-cell plot turns the U.S. president into the mastermind behind a White House terror attack.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The premise has immediate, trailer-friendly escalation: border patrol, drug cartel, White House siege, and a presidential betrayal. The marketability is real, but the script’s overtly inflammatory political framing and broad, pulpy execution narrow the buyer pool.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The hook lands early: John Scout, Fernando Rey, and a national-security crisis collide almost immediately. The later reveal that the president is the terrorist leader is clear and memorable, even if the script keeps stacking twists rather than deepening the central premise.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Scout has a clean action-hero spine, Rey has swagger, and Emillo gives the story a smart-ass pressure valve. But the characters are built more as functions in the machine than as fully surprising people, so the emotional attachment is limited.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script is bold in its willingness to make the president the villain and to fuse cartel action with domestic-terror spectacle. The execution is more sensational than fresh, though, and several reversals lean on shock value rather than a singular point of view.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: Once the siege begins, the script keeps moving: tunnel escape, White House assault, nuclear-plant finale. The momentum is strong, but the middle section is heavy on briefing and repetition before the final run turns fully propulsive.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The core idea of a sitting president as the hidden terrorist leader is instantly legible and commercially provocative. What keeps it from scoring higher is that the surrounding material feels familiar in its action-thriller beats and its broad good-guy/bad-guy reversals.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: There’s useful texture in the border station, the drug tunnel network, the White House security apparatus, and the San Onofrio plant. Still, most of the world exists to service the plot, not to generate a deeper social system.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The tone is consistent in its loud, hard-charging, pulp-action register. It doesn’t yet have a singular tonal signature beyond escalation, outrage, and patriotic spectacle.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: The script is built for immediate payoff, not layered ambiguity. The political and identity material is provocative, but it’s presented bluntly, so there’s not much sense of hidden depth beneath the surface.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: Scout/Emillo and Scout/Rey give the script a workable two-pair engine, and Kinney adds a solid institutional counterweight. But the supporting cast mostly serves plot turns, so the relationship web doesn’t generate much beyond the main action.

lead_characters.name: John Scout
lead_characters.demographics: Male, late 20s to early 30s, border patrol officer, Native American-coded by the script’s language and surrounding characters.
lead_characters.hook: A rugged border patrol officer who starts the story in a domestic groove and ends it as a furious, grief-struck avenger. Scout is blunt, physically capable, and emotionally guarded; the script gives him a clean action-hero arc, but his real engine is betrayal — by his fiancée, by his job, and by the country he serves.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of a young Gerard Butler or Josh Brolin in a breakout action lead — a physically commanding role that also asks for wounded restraint, rage, and moral whiplash.

lead_characters.name: Fernando Rey
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 30s-40s, Mexican drug lord, charismatic, well-dressed, bilingual.
lead_characters.hook: A drug kingpin with enough intelligence and self-regard to read as a statesman in his own criminal kingdom. Rey is the script’s most watchable wildcard: he’s ruthless, funny, strategic, and unexpectedly patriotic when the threat becomes existential.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Benicio del Toro in Sicario or Javier Bardem in No Country for Old Men their scene-stealing authority — a cool, dangerous operator with wit, menace, and command.

lead_characters.name: Emillo Cortz
lead_characters.demographics: Male, early 20s, Latino, hacker, college-age intelligence type.
lead_characters.hook: Rey’s bookish nephew and the story’s tech translator, Emillo is the smart, anxious, slightly comic bridge between the street-level and the digital conspiracy. He’s not built as a deep emotional lead, but he gives the script its fastest dialogue and its clearest modern utility.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that let Jesse Eisenberg or Lakeith Stanfield play speed, intelligence, and nervous humor at once — a sharp supporting turn with real scene-stealing potential.

lead_characters.name: Malcom Kinney
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 50s, FBI Director, seasoned institutional authority.
lead_characters.hook: A calm, weary federal operator who becomes the story’s moral and procedural anchor as the White House collapses around him. Kinney is the adult in the room, but the script also gives him enough pressure and physical jeopardy to keep him from becoming pure exposition.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Jeffrey Wright in political thrillers or Tommy Lee Jones in The Fugitive their gravitas — a controlled, intelligent authority figure with late-game heroism.

lead_characters.name: Beau Dama
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 50s, African-American president, public-facing statesman with hidden extremist allegiance.
lead_characters.hook: A polished, calm, deeply duplicitous president whose public unity rhetoric masks a catastrophic ideological agenda. Dama is the script’s biggest swing: he starts as a national leader and ends as the story’s most shocking betrayal, which makes him a potent but highly polarizing figure.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of prestige-villain role that lets an actor play charm, authority, and ideological rot in one package — the showcase territory of a Bryan Cranston or Michael Shannon turn.

lead_characters.name: Faruk Pink
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 30s-40s, presidential aide, Muslim-coded, cyber/intelligence specialist.
lead_characters.hook: The president’s trusted aide and the story’s quiet conduit between power and covert operations. Pink is one of the script’s key suspicion engines: he looks like administration muscle, but the story keeps using him as a signal that the real conspiracy is deeper than the room in front of us.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the pleasure of controlled ambiguity — the sort of part that can play like a Peter Sarsgaard or Riz Ahmed supporting turn, where stillness becomes threat.

lead_characters.name: Imani Chaqueri
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 20s-30s, Scout’s fiancée, secretly tied to the terrorist network.
lead_characters.hook: Scout’s intimate emotional anchor and the story’s most painful betrayal. Imani is written as seductive, intelligent, and tragic, with the script using her as both romantic ideal and ideological reveal; she’s less developed than the men around her, but she carries the story’s emotional knife twist.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actress a late-reveal pivot, like Rebecca Hall in a thriller or Rosamund Pike in a betrayal story — the chance to shift from romantic presence to devastating reveal.

lead_characters.name: Brock Lindbergh
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 50s-60s, Vice President turned President, military background.
lead_characters.hook: A disciplined, suspicious vice president who becomes the story’s emergency successor and final public face of restoration. Lindbergh is a functional authority role, but the script uses him effectively as the man who gets to narrate the victory after the chaos.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of late-stage authority role that lets an actor land a clean, patriotic button — the sort of part that gives gravitas without requiring a full emotional arc.

casting_characteristics: Multiple military, federal, and terrorist ensemble roles
Several roles require bilingual or accent-specific performance
One major presidential role and one major drug-lord role are both highly specific star-casting opportunities

notable_requirements: White House interiors and exterior siege coverage
Border patrol station and desert tunnel build
San Onofrio nuclear power plant exterior and containment interior
Washington D.C. and New York City street coverage

technical.vfx_details: Explosion work, White House attack coverage, nuclear-plant destruction, helicopter and aircraft inserts, crowd-control enhancement, and large-scale fire/smoke elements.
technical.sfx_needs: Gunfire choreography, suicide-bomber practical effects, vehicle impacts, tunnel demolition, and large-scale explosion rigs.

rights_flags.detail: BTO's 'Gimme Your Money Please' is specifically named and would need music clearance if retained.
Rolling Stone is referenced in dialogue as the source of Rey's notoriety and may require trademark review depending on final usage.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release with broad action-thriller positioning; best suited to a theatrical or premium-streaming event model.

budget.note: White House siege coverage, nuclear-plant action, multiple large-scale gun battles, vehicle stunts, and explosion-heavy set pieces will push this well above a contained indie action budget.

casting.note: Scout, Rey, and Dama are all highly specific roles with strong star-vehicle potential, and the script also needs credible military/federal ensemble casting across several authority figures.

development.note: The script’s political provocation, the president-as-terrorist reveal, and the broad ideological framing create a buyer conversation about tone, audience, and sensitivity before any packaging conversation can close.

comp_set.title: Olympus Has Fallen
comp_set.why_it_comps: Shares the White House-under-siege spectacle, patriotic rescue mechanics, and a muscular action-forward release posture.

comp_set.title: Sicario
comp_set.why_it_comps: The border-crime texture, morally compromised alliances, and hard-edged law-enforcement perspective are the closest tonal neighbors.

comp_set.title: Air Force One
comp_set.why_it_comps: Like this script, it turns presidential vulnerability and national-security panic into a high-concept action engine.

comp_set.title: The Kingdom
comp_set.why_it_comps: The counterterrorism urgency, ensemble federal response, and geopolitical tension map cleanly onto the script’s structure.

audience_target.primary_audience: Adult action-thriller viewers who want high-stakes patriotism, conspiracy reveals, and large-scale siege spectacle.
audience_target.demographics: Primarily men 25-54, with secondary appeal to women 25-44 who respond to political thrillers and star-driven action.

budget_tier.note: The budget is driven by multiple action set pieces, White House and nuclear-plant coverage, vehicle work, and crowd/explosion logistics.

lane_fit.detail: This sits in the lane of elevated-but-pulpy action with a clear hook and a recognizable patriotic crisis engine. The combination of federal institutions, cartel muscle, and a presidential betrayal gives it a sellable poster and a straightforward trailer cut.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature: Scout, Rey, and Kinney have enough presence for one strong outing, but the story resolves its central conspiracy and does not establish a clean franchise vector.

strengths.what_it_means: A buyer can understand the movie in one sentence and immediately see the trailer shape, which is a real advantage in a crowded action-thriller market. That makes it attractive to studio genre execs and streamer buyers looking for a clear, high-concept event without needing a long pitch.
strengths.evidence: The story quickly reveals a border patrol officer, a drug lord, a White House siege, and a president who is secretly the terrorist leader.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The central betrayal is a strong engine.
strengths.what_it_means: Scout’s fiancée, his sergeant, and the president all turn out to be part of the same conspiracy web, which gives the script a built-in betrayal cascade. That kind of emotional and political reversal is what makes a thriller feel like a must-discuss title for genre audiences.
strengths.evidence: Imani’s reveal at the condo, Connor’s unmasking in the tunnel, and Dama’s final turn at the plant all reframe the story.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Rey is a breakout supporting role.
strengths.what_it_means: The movie has a scene-stealing secondary character who can help sell the package and give the film a memorable face beyond the lead. Buyers like this because it creates casting leverage and gives the movie a quotable, poster-friendly wild card.
strengths.evidence: Rey is funny, ruthless, strategic, and unexpectedly patriotic, especially in the tunnel and at the nuclear plant.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The set pieces are easy to market.
strengths.what_it_means: The White House siege, the tunnel battle, and the nuclear-plant finale are all visually legible action beats that can be sold in a trailer and international materials. That gives the project a commercial spine even before casting.
strengths.evidence: The script moves from border station siege to White House assault to San Onofrio showdown.

strengths.what_it_means: The FBI, CIA, Pentagon, White House, and border patrol all create a layered authority stack that makes the world feel bigger than the lead’s personal story. That helps the movie feel like an event rather than a single-location thriller.
strengths.evidence: Kinney, Salt, King, Ramone, and the military brass all have distinct positions in the crisis response.

whats_special.headline: This is a clean, high-concept action-thriller package with a trailer-ready hook, a scene-stealing cartel wildcard, and multiple large-scale set pieces that justify a mid-budget event play. The commercial upside is strongest for buyers who want a patriotic siege movie with a sharp betrayal engine and enough spectacle to travel internationally.

items.area: The president-as-terrorist swing is a buyer filter.
items.detail: Beau Dama’s reveal as the mastermind is the script’s biggest hook, but it also makes the movie politically volatile and tonally aggressive. Some buyers will see that as a selling point; others will see it as a hard stop depending on platform brand and audience strategy.

items.area: The action footprint is not cheap.
items.detail: The White House siege, the tunnel battle, the motorcade attack, and the nuclear-plant finale all ask for substantial practical coverage, stunt coordination, and explosion work. This is not a contained action piece; it needs real scope to land.

items.area: Imani is more twist than person.
items.detail: Her condo reveal is effective, but the script uses her primarily as a betrayal mechanism rather than a fully dimensional character. That limits the emotional aftershock of Scout’s loss and narrows the role’s casting appeal beyond the reveal itself.

items.area: The middle section leans on briefing.
items.detail: A substantial stretch of the script is government rooms, security updates, and explanatory dialogue before the action fully detonates. That keeps the premise clear, but it also slows the momentum relative to the scale of the finale.

items.area: The tonal register is broad and blunt.
items.detail: The script plays its reversals, slogans, and ideological reveals at full volume, which gives it heat but not much shading. Buyers looking for a more nuanced political thriller will likely read this as pulp first and prestige second.

issues.headline: The main friction is that the script’s biggest commercial asset is also its biggest sensitivity: the president-as-terrorist reveal is unforgettable, but it sharply narrows the buyer conversation. Beyond that, the movie needs real action money and a buyer comfortable with broad, politically charged pulp rather than subtle thriller terrain.
